subject: mathematics
question_text: If A + B = π/4, prove that (a) (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B) = 2 and (b) (cot A − 1)(cot B − 1) = 2.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 8 TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS, Very Short Answer question 31(ii), book p.88. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The book prints the two lettered parts under one condition, so they stay in one card and the 1 + 1 gives one mark to each part. Part (a) needs tan A and tan B to exist and part (b) needs cot A and cot B to exist; the two conditions are different and each is written into its own step. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A prints ten very short answers of 2 marks each and the student writes all ten, under the 2026-27 pattern; Trigonometric Ratios and Transformations supplies two of those ten slots. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove both parts — name the formula each part starts from.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Part (a) from tan(A + B) = 1
steps.margin_note: First mark. tan(π/4) = 1 makes the numerator equal the denominator, which gives tan A + tan B + tan A tan B = 1 — exactly the three terms the bracket produces.
steps.memory_tip: tan(π/4) = 1, so tan A + tan B = 1 − tan A tan B. Expanding the bracket gives 1 plus that same sum.
lines: (a) For tan A and tan B to exist, neither
A nor B is an odd multiple of π/2.
⇒ (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B) = 1
⇒ tan A + tan B + tan A tan B = 1
= 1 + (tan A + tan B + tan A tan B)

recall.must_convey: That tan(A + B) = 1 gives tan A + tan B + tan A tan B = 1, and that expanding the bracket produces 1 plus that sum.
accept: tan of pi by four is one so the numerator equals the denominator
tan A plus tan B plus tan A tan B equals one
expand the bracket and you get one plus that sum
tan pi by four one kabatti, mottam sum one avthundi
reject: cot of pi by four is one

steps.why: tan(π/4) = 1 turns the given condition into tan A + tan B + tan A tan B = 1, and that sum is exactly the three extra terms produced by expanding (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B). The expansion and the condition give the same three terms, which is why the proof is short.
common_mistakes: Expanding (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B) as 1 + tan A tan B.
Stopping at tan A + tan B = 1 − tan A tan B without expanding the bracket.

steps.label: Part (b) from cot(A + B) = 1
steps.margin_note: Second mark. cot(π/4) = 1 as well. Work in cotangents directly — turning every cotangent into 1/tan makes the algebra much longer.
steps.memory_tip: cot(π/4) = 1 too. Use the cotangent addition formula so no fraction is ever created.
lines: (b) For cot A and cot B to exist, neither
A nor B is a multiple of π.
⇒ (cot A cot B − 1)/(cot A + cot B) = 1
⇒ cot A cot B − cot A − cot B = 1
= cot A cot B − cot A − cot B + 1

recall.must_convey: That cot(A + B) = 1 gives cot A cot B − cot A − cot B = 1, and that expanding the bracket produces that expression plus 1.
accept: cot of pi by four is one so use the cot addition formula
cot A cot B minus cot A minus cot B equals one
expand the bracket and add one
cot formula vaadithe fraction raadu, direct ga vasthundi
reject: tan A plus tan B plus tan A tan B equals one

steps.why: Part (b) is part (a) written in cotangents. Starting from the cotangent addition formula keeps every term a whole cotangent, so no fractions appear; replacing each cot by 1/tan reaches the same answer through much longer algebra.
common_mistakes: Writing cot(A + B) = (cot A cot B + 1)/(cot A + cot B).
Expanding (cot A − 1)(cot B − 1) without the +1 term.
